newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish credit growth too high for comfort-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Irish credit growth too high for comfort-analysts.

text.p: Irish private sector credit growth remained too high for comfort in July and was likely to add to nervousness in the money market, analysts said.
End-month banking statistics released on Thursday showed that private sector credit grew by 13.7 percent in July, up from 13.3 percent in June.

The growth rate was in line with market forecasts, most of which were in the 13.5 to 14.0 percent range. Analysts said the market had priced in a strong figure but noted that July was the sixth consecutive month to see an increase in the overall growth rate, which was unlikely to please the central bank.

"It certainly isn't going to reduce nervousness in the money markets," Colin Hunt, economist at Bank of Ireland Group Treasury, told Reuters. "Where monetary policy goes from here, that's the question that has to be asked now."
Analysts say the central bank is likely to be concerned about the continued high rate of credit growth, particularly mortgage lending which was up by 16.1 percent in July.

Following a higher-than-expected credit growth rate in June, the bank allowed money market rates to move higher, triggering retail interest rate rises by four of Ireland's leading lending institutions.
"Underlying credit growth remains too high for comfort, running well above the central bank's implicit 7.5 percent target for the year," Alan McQuaid of Bloxham Stockbrokers said.
He said there was growing optimism in the financial markets that the recent 25 basis point rise in retail rates would be the only domestic interest rate increase this year.

"However, in our view the outlook for the rest of 1996 is uncertain. The expected pick up in services inflation coupled with the continuing strong growth in credit demand could force the central bank to engineer another rise in retail rates before the year is out," McQuaid said in a research note.
But others believe that a further rate rise is unlikely against a background of falling interest rates across Europe.

"You have seen Irish interest rates move up at the time core Europe has moved down, despite the fact that Ireland is a credible contender for entry into EMU from the begining," said Ulster Bank's Fahy.

"This type of trend we've seen is probably priced in, that's why there's a premium of nearly three percent in short term Irish rates over German rates. I think it's well discounted and I don't believe there will be a further move upwards in short term rates as a result of this."

After the data, the five-year benchmark government bond slipped to 103.50 to yield 6.86 from 103.58 before the data. Further out on the curve, 10-year paper edged back to 102.60 to yield 7.48 pct from 102.66.
On the money market, the key one-month money market rate was trading at 5.56/5.69 percent.

The end-month banking data also showed a fall of 177 million Irish pounds in the official external reserves in July. Analysts were expecting a fall of 100-200 million following rumours the central bank intervened to support the Irish pound in July.
But the bank attributed the drop to interest and principal payments on the Exchequer foreign debt which exceeded EU transfers and net positive foreign-exchange market intervention.
"I don't think that was expected in the markets, I think that has surprised the markets," said Fahy.
